strengths: The task is well motivated: combining a reference person's appearance with a description of changed clothing provides information unavailable to either modality alone. ITCPR, with 2,202 queries and a 20,510-image gallery, is a potentially useful community resource.

Word4Per offers a simple, coherent approach using person-specific CLIP fine-tuning followed by lightweight textual inversion. Training uses existing image-text and identity annotations without requiring CPR triplets.
The improvements over straightforward fusion are substantial. With ViT-L/14, joint supervision achieves 45.91% Rank-1 and 55.63% mAP, compared with 32.02% and 41.83% for image/text feature averaging.

The paper includes extensive ablations on supervision, architecture, training-data quantity, prompts, token counts, and ensembles. Pipeline diagrams, optimization settings, hardware specifications, and runtime measurements help explain the method and support reproduction.
weaknesses: The strongest baseline comparisons are confounded. Table I evaluates Pic2Word and SEARLE inversion networks trained with original CLIP alongside fine-tuned encoders, whereas Word4Per's inversion network is trained for those adapted encoders. The disclosed representation mismatch could substantially disadvantage the baselines. Retraining competing methods with matched encoders and person data is necessary to establish the claimed methodological advantage.

The evaluation does not establish an untouched test protocol. Section IV designates ITCPR exclusively for testing, yet Figure 7 and Table V use its results to select architecture and prompt configurations. No separate validation or source-only model-selection procedure is described. Missing repeated-seed results or uncertainty estimates also make small ablation and ensemble improvements difficult to assess.

Benchmark reliability needs stronger evidence. Missing positives are discovered through visual retrieval followed by manual inspection, but the retrieval encoder, candidate depth, annotation agreement, and residual false-negative audit are unspecified. This procedure does not establish that all relevant matches were recovered. Source-wise and modification-type results would also clarify generalization beyond the preferentially selected partial clothing changes.

Methodological originality is incremental: pseudo-word inversion follows established zero-shot CIR approaches, while CLIP adaptation uses existing SDM and identity objectives. Adding textual supervision to visual supervision improves ViT-L/14 Rank-1 from 43.96% to 45.91%, considerably less than the headline comparison suggests. The task and dataset therefore carry much of the contribution, making their validation especially important.

The mechanistic explanations exceed the evidence. Attention maps from the frozen visual encoder describe TINet's input, rather than establishing what TINet preserves or suppresses. A few retrieval examples and nearest-vocabulary words do not demonstrate reliable background suppression or identity preservation; controlled interventions and systematic failure analysis are missing.

The proposed dataset release and public-security applications involve identifiable people, but the manuscript does not document source-data redistribution permissions, consent/privacy constraints, or surveillance misuse considerations. These are relevant omissions in the research documentation, although the manuscript does not establish a specific ethical violation.
